scenarios.title: Validate a retry window
scenarios.summary: Reject unsafe numeric arguments before calculating a retry plan.
scenarios.objective: Write a script receiving ATTEMPTS and DELAY as two arguments. ATTEMPTS is one decimal digit, 1–8. DELAY is 0–300 seconds, written using ordinary digits 0–9 with no leading zeros except 0. Print Attempts, Delay and Wait window as three “Label: value” lines. Wait window is (ATTEMPTS − 1) × DELAY. On a wrong argument count, print “Usage: retry-plan ATTEMPTS DELAY”; otherwise reject attempts first, then delay, using the exact Invalid messages shown in the cases. Errors go to stderr with status 2 and no stdout. Preserve all simulated files.

scenarios.explanation:
Validate argument count and text shape first. A small accepted width prevents overflow-sized inputs from reaching integer operations. Bound delay to 300, then calculate one fewer waiting interval than attempts.

One supported solution, available on request:
decimal3() {
  case "$1" in
    ''|*[!0-9]*|0?*|????*) return 1 ;;
    *) return 0 ;;
  esac
}
if test "$#" -ne 2; then
  printf 'Usage: retry-plan ATTEMPTS DELAY\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
case "$1" in
  [1-8]) true ;;
  *) printf 'Invalid attempts: use 1 through 8.\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
if decimal3 "$2"; then
  if test "$2" -gt 300; then
    printf 'Invalid delay: use 0 through 300 without leading zeros.\n' >&2
    exit 2
  fi
else
  printf 'Invalid delay: use 0 through 300 without leading zeros.\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
wait=$(( ($1 - 1) * $2 ))
printf 'Attempts: %s\nDelay: %s\nWait window: %s\n' "$1" "$2" "$wait"
hints: Start with the argument count, then validate attempts so the error order is predictable.
An allowlist of exact digit widths rejects empty, signed, non-ASCII, leading-zero and overlong values without arithmetic.
After text is safe, enforce DELAY ≤300. An initial attempt does not require a preceding delay.
scenarios.simplifications: Portable shell syntax within the bounded in-process subset, in fixed C/POSIX locale. ASCII digits only; no fractions, signs, base# conversion, regex, Unicode digit classification or arbitrary precision. Files are virtual UTF-8 text in flat /work; no host commands/files/network. This unit rejects leading zeros deliberately; it does not claim Bash rejects every leading-zero number. Validation before a single output write is not an operating-system atomic-rename or crash-recovery guarantee.

concepts.title: Numbers arrive as text
concepts.text: The lab supplies $1 and $2 as arguments. A blank, 12x or a very long run of digits is still text. Validate it before using test -gt or arithmetic. You create working variables such as wait; they are not supplied answers.

concepts.title: A class describes one position
concepts.text: In case, [0-9] matches one ordinary digit from 0 through 9 (ASCII). Other numeral shapes, such as ３, are not part of this rule. [1-9][0-9] matches a two-digit value without a leading zero. A pattern matches the whole value. Alternatives use |; the first matching arm runs.

concepts.title: A star does not repeat the digit rule
concepts.text: [0-9]* means a digit followed by anything, so 3x matches it. To detect any non-digit, use *[!0-9]*. Handle an empty value separately. Quoted values remain data, even when they look like shell code.

concepts.title: Check spelling and width before value
concepts.text: For at most two digits, accept 0, [1-9] or [1-9][0-9]. This bounds the text before a numeric test. For three digits, add a third explicit digit position. Then enforce the smaller practical limit required by the task.

concepts.title: Leading zero has a different meaning in arithmetic
concepts.text: Shell arithmetic can treat 010 as octal eight, and 08 is not valid octal. Very large arithmetic values can wrap. This unit deliberately accepts only ordinary decimal spelling and small limits, so neither case reaches arithmetic.

concepts.title: Explain a rejected request
concepts.text: A useful error says which input to fix, goes to stderr with >&2 and exits with status 2. A valid request exits0. The separate example checks its own working variable; your assignment must check the lab-supplied arguments.

teaching.example:
decimal2() {
  case "$1" in
    0|[1-9]|[1-9][0-9]) return 0 ;;
    *) return 1 ;;
  esac
}
slots=14
if decimal2 "$slots"; then
  doubled=$((slots * 2))
  printf 'Double: %s\n' "$doubled"
else
  printf 'Use 0 through 99 without leading zeros.\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
teaching.inputs: The example creates slots=14 itself; it has no supplied arguments. A separate virtual badge-notes.txt must remain unchanged. The decimal2 helper reports success or failure before multiplication.
teaching.try_change: Change slots=14 to slots=014 and Run example. It should print a useful error instead of multiplying an octal-looking value. Restore 14 to repair the example.

scenarios.retry_guidance: An unsupported integer/arithmetic operand can mean input reached numeric work too early. Check its spelling and width first. For valid requests, count the gaps between attempts.

scenarios.explanation:
Keep raw rows intact, then classify them as bounded canonical decimals. Record position is independent of acceptance. Reporting invalid data is a successful implementation of this assignment when output, status and unchanged files match all cases.

One supported solution, available on request:
decimal3() {
  case "$1" in
    ''|*[!0-9]*|0?*|????*) return 1 ;;
    *) return 0 ;;
  esac
}
if test "$#" -ne 1; then
  printf 'Usage: intake-audit SOURCE\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
if test -f "$1"; then true
else printf 'Cannot audit: source is missing.\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
line=0
accepted=0
rejected=0
total=0
while IFS= read -r row || test -n "$row"; do
  line=$((line + 1))
  if decimal3 "$row"; then
    accepted=$((accepted + 1))
    total=$((total + row))
  else
    rejected=$((rejected + 1))
    printf 'Rejected line %s: %s\n' "$line" "$row" >&2
  fi
done < "$1"
printf 'Accepted: %s\nRejected: %s\nTotal: %s\n' "$accepted" "$rejected" "$total"
if test "$rejected" -eq 0; then exit 0; else exit 1; fi
hints: Reuse a text-only numeric check before adding a row to total. Empty, space-padded and non-ASCII rows are invalid.
Use the line-preserving read/EOF pattern from the prerequisite. Do not pipe the loop if its counters are needed afterward.
The complete audit prints its summary even after bad rows; missing input or wrong arguments are different preflight errors.

concepts.title: Choose recovery deliberately
concepts.text: A bad request may require stopping. An intake audit instead records the problem and keeps inspecting later rows. Do not add rejected text to the total, and do not let a malformed row become an arithmetic error.

concepts.title: Preserve the text you diagnose
concepts.text: IFS= read -r row keeps edge spaces and backslashes so a report can show what was actually supplied. Plain read can trim spaces and accidentally turn a rejected row into a valid number. LF separates records; a carriage return remains part of the row.

concepts.title: Do not lose the last record
concepts.text: read assigns a final nonempty line without LF but returns failure. The existing while pattern “IFS= read -r row || test -n "$row"” processes that last value too. An empty file has no records; a blank line is one rejected record.

concepts.title: Count position and acceptance separately
concepts.text: Advance the line number for every record. Advance the accepted count and total only after its text passes the numeric rule. Advance the rejected count and print an error for every other row; no break or continue is required.

concepts.title: An error report can be the correct solution
concepts.text: Exit 1 means the audit found rejected records, not that your script is necessarily wrong. The lab expects that status for those sample files. Syntax/unsupported diagnostics are different: the script should handle bad data itself.

teaching.example:
checked=0
flagged=0
while IFS= read -r label || test -n "$label"; do
  case "$label" in
    [0-9]) checked=$((checked + 1)) ;;
    *) flagged=$((flagged + 1)) ;;
  esac
done < "labels.txt"
printf 'Labels checked: %s\nLabels to review: %s\n' "$checked" "$flagged"
teaching.inputs: The example reads its own labels.txt, containing 3, 12 and x. It creates checked and flagged counters. These files and counters are separate from assignment drafts and inputs.
teaching.try_change: Change the accepted pattern [0-9] to [0-9]|[1-9][0-9]. Run example: two labels now pass and one needs review. Restore the single-digit pattern to repair it.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Rejected data rows are expected in some cases. Compare line numbers, exact original text, accepted totals and status. Syntax/unsupported diagnostics are different failures. Continue after malformed rows.

scenarios.title: Preview a safe batch allocation
scenarios.summary: Validate every amount and the whole budget before changing an existing plan.
scenarios.objective: Write a script receiving MODE, BUDGET, SOURCE and DESTINATION as four arguments. MODE is preview or publish. BUDGET is 0–999 in ordinary decimal without leading zeros except 0. Use simple filenames: nonempty, no slash, not . or .. or -. SOURCE must exist and differ from DESTINATION. Each source line is a job requesting 1–99 units in the same decimal spelling; inspect a final line without LF too. An empty file is a valid zero-job plan. Reject the first bad row or a total above budget. On success, build the five-line Source/Jobs/Units/Budget/Remaining report shown in the cases. Preview prints that report and changes nothing. Publish writes it to DESTINATION with one final newline and prints “Created: NAME”. Any rejection is status 2, stderr only and every file unchanged. Validate in order: argument count, mode, budget, source name, destination name, collision, source existence, row order, total budget.

scenarios.explanation:
Preflight arguments and names, validate all source rows, then compare the total. A capture or a separate validation pass can delay publication. Any valid supported design passes when its output, status and entire virtual file map match, including rejected and preview requests.

One supported solution, available on request:
decimal3() {
  case "$1" in
    ''|*[!0-9]*|0?*|????*) return 1 ;;
    *) return 0 ;;
  esac
}
if test "$#" -ne 4; then
  printf 'Usage: plan MODE BUDGET SOURCE DESTINATION\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
case "$1" in
  preview|publish) true ;;
  *) printf 'Mode must be preview or publish.\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
if decimal3 "$2"; then true
else printf 'Invalid budget: use 0 through 999 without leading zeros.\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
case "$3" in
  ''|.|..|-|*/*) printf 'Invalid source name.\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
  *) true ;;
esac
case "$4" in
  ''|.|..|-|*/*) printf 'Invalid destination name.\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
  *) true ;;
esac
if test "$3" = "$4"; then
  printf 'Source and destination must differ.\n' >&2
  exit 2
fi
if test -f "$3"; then true
else printf 'Cannot plan: source is missing.\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
mode=$1
budget=$2
source=$3
destination=$4
build_plan() {
  line=0
  jobs=0
  units=0
  while IFS= read -r row || test -n "$row"; do
    line=$((line + 1))
    case "$row" in
      [1-9]|[1-9][0-9]) true ;;
      *) printf 'Invalid units on line %s: use 1 through 99 without leading zeros.\n' "$line" >&2; return 2 ;;
    esac
    jobs=$((jobs + 1))
    units=$((units + row))
  done < "$1"
  if test "$units" -gt "$2"; then
    printf 'Batch exceeds budget.\n' >&2
    return 2
  fi
  allowance=$2
  remaining=$((allowance - units))
  printf 'Source: %s\nJobs: %s\nUnits: %s\nBudget: %s\nRemaining: %s\n' "$1" "$jobs" "$units" "$allowance" "$remaining"
}
report=$(build_plan "$source" "$budget") || exit 2
if test "$mode" = preview; then
  printf '%s\n' "$report"
else
  printf '%s\n' "$report" > "$destination"
  printf 'Created: %s\n' "$destination"
fi
hints: Handle argument and mode errors before interpreting any budget text. Bound its spelling before using a numeric comparison.
Use the previous unit’s read and numeric checks, but stop with the first bad row instead of publishing a partial allocation.
Keep report construction before the only destination write. Capture strips trailing LF, so restore exactly one with printf. A direct validate-then-print solution also works.

concepts.title: Decide whether partial work is useful
concepts.text: The intake audit could continue after bad data. An approved allocation cannot contain partial or invalid amounts. Here a bad row or an over-budget total must leave the existing plan exactly as it was.

concepts.title: Validate the interface before reading
concepts.text: Check mode and budget before source/destination names. This lab deliberately uses simple flat virtual filenames, not general Linux path handling. A quoted filename remains one value even when it contains spaces, a dash or a literal star.

concepts.title: Validate amounts before adding them
concepts.text: Each job needs1–99 units; 0 is not a valid job size. Match one or two digit positions without leading zero before adding. Count every accepted job, including a final line without LF, then compare the total with the already validated budget.

concepts.title: Build before publishing
concepts.text: The existing report=$(build_plan ...) form captures a function’s output and removes trailing LF. Keep all errors on stderr; on rejection return 2 before printing a report. Use || to stop publication when that function fails. A separate validate-then-print approach is equally valid.

concepts.title: Preview and publish share one decision
concepts.text: Both modes must accept or reject the same input. Preview prints the validated report but never writes the destination. Publish uses printf with a fixed %s format and a final newline to write the full report only after validation.

concepts.title: Be precise about safety
concepts.text: This practice protects virtual input and unrelated files from mistaken early writes. It does not implement operating-system temporary files, atomic rename, crashes or resumable jobs. Portable syntax here does not mean every shell feature is supported.

teaching.example:
make_notice() {
  seats=0
  while IFS= read -r row || test -n "$row"; do
    case "$row" in
      [1-9]) seats=$((seats + row)) ;;
      *) printf 'Room entry needs review.\n' >&2; return 2 ;;
    esac
  done < "rooms.txt"
  if test "$seats" -gt 8; then
    printf 'Room limit exceeded.\n' >&2
    return 2
  fi
  printf 'Seats requested: %s\n' "$seats"
}
mode=preview
notice=$(make_notice) || exit 2
if test "$mode" = publish; then
  printf '%s\n' "$notice" > "room-notice.txt"
  printf 'Saved example notice.\n'
else
  printf '%s\n' "$notice"
fi
teaching.inputs: The example creates mode=preview and reads its own rooms.txt. Its limit is 8 seats, not the assignment budget interface. room-notice.txt initially contains an older notice and must stay unchanged in preview.
teaching.try_change: Change mode=preview to mode=publish and Run example. Only the example room-notice.txt should change; assignment files and credit stay untouched. Restore preview to repair the example.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the file map as well as stdout. Preview and every rejection must preserve old plans. A plausible report does not compensate for an early write during a failed request.
